query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Friction stir processing (FSP) of the as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy will simultaneously improve its room-temperature tensile ductility and strength relative to the unmodified dual-phase lamellar microstructure by refining inter-lamellar boundaries through localized dynamic recrystallization.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar colony structure (e.g., fcc/B2) featuring numerous rigid internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply friction stir processing (FSP) under controlled processing parameters to the as-cast alloy.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading with FSP parameters tuned to induce localized dynamic recrystallization without changing the overall phase constitution; the intervention is applied as a single treatment on the as-cast alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined inter-lamellar boundaries and a graded interfacial grain structure resulting from localized dynamic recrystallization.
generation.mechanism: FSP generates severe plastic deformation along with moderate local heating, which induces dynamic recrystallization specifically at inter-lamellar boundaries. This modification reduces stress concentrations by producing more coherent and ductile interfaces that hinder microcrack nucleation and promote effective load transfer, thereby enhancing both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the FSP-treated alloy should display higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths and an increased tensile strain to failure due to reduced microcrack initiation at the refined interfacial regions.
generation.baseline: The untreated as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibits high room-temperature strength but limited ductility because of brittle, microcrack-prone dual-phase lamellar interfaces.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are limited to processing conditions that achieve sufficient interfacial refinement without over-aging or coarsening the microstructure. The improvements are expected under room-temperature tensile conditions and for the alloy system with a maintained dual-phase (fcc/B2) architecture.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in strength and ductility depend on optimizing FSP parameters, and there is uncertainty regarding the magnitude of the interface modifications achievable without altering phase balance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set will be processed using optimized FSP parameters, and the other set will remain as-cast. Perform detailed room-temperature tensile testing and microscopic characterization (e.g., TEM, SEM) to evaluate interfacial grain structure and measure mechanical properties.
measurements: TEM/SEM characterization of inter-lamellar boundary morphology and grain size distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSP-treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the as-cast samples, or if microstructural analyses do not show refined and more cohesive inter-lamellar boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] . decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (e.g., in PMC4145285) focused on obtaining high strength through conventional melting and thermomechanical treatments (cold rolling, directional solidification) that refined the lamellar colony architecture. These methods improved yield strength but did little to arrest microcrack initiation along the numerous phase boundaries, so the ductility was compromised. Subsequent studies tried to modify phase distribution and precipitation features, yet the underlying problem of brittle inter-lamellar interfaces causing catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile loading remained largely unsolved.
decision.unsolved: The persistent challenge is the inability to simultaneously improve strength and room-temperature ductility because the dual-phase lamellar microstructure inherently possesses internal boundaries that act as sites for microcrack initiation. No single intervention to tailor the interfacial behavior to both resist microcracking and enhance load transfer has been definitively demonstrated.
decision.lever: Apply friction stir processing (FSP) to the as-cast eutectic HEA to selectively modify the inter-lamellar boundaries by inducing localized dynamic recrystallization and refined interfacial grain structures
decision.why: FSP is a processing technique that, by generating a controlled severe plastic deformation and moderate local heat input, can restructure the internal boundaries without altering the overall composition. It is expected to improve interfacial cohesion by reducing stress concentrations and promoting a graded, more ductile interface, thereby mitigating microcrack initiation while retaining or enhancing strength. This approach follows the historical trend where conventional treatments have addressed overall strength but not interfacial brittleness, making targeted interface engineering via FSP a plausible next intervention.
